title: Cumulative Review 4: Modules 1 to 12
intro: Spaced review mixes questions from earlier modules. Retrieving older material now is what makes it stick. Items you miss come back for a retry round.

items.why: Noise in the scores weakens the observable association, which is why reliability matters.

items.q: In a class of 400 students, 40 are chosen at random and their mean exam score is 78. The class mean is 80. This 2 point gap is
items.why: Random samples differ from the population by chance. A small gap like this is exactly what sampling error looks like.

items.q: For the same study, Cohen's d is the mean difference divided by sigma. What is d?
items.why: d = (79 minus 75)/12 = .33, a small to medium effect. The z of 2.00 mixes effect size with sample size.

o: Variance between groups divided by variance within groups
Variance within divided by variance between
The mean difference divided by SD
SS total divided by SS between
items.why: F = MS between divided by MS within. Under the null it is near 1.

items.q: A 2 by 2 design has how many cells?
items.why: Multiply the number of levels of each factor.

items.q: A researcher says, "Because my groups were not significantly different, they must have had equal means." What is wrong?
o: The sample means differed by 5. The test only shows the difference is not distinguishable from sampling error
The groups should have been larger
The mean difference is the standard error
items.why: Non-significance concerns the population. The sample means still differ, and the data are compatible with a real difference.

items.q: In a scatterplot, a strong positive linear relationship looks like
o: Points close to a line rising from lower left to upper right
Points close to a line falling
items.why: The tighter the points cluster around the line, the larger the absolute value of r.

items.q: Which sample mean is more surprising if the population mean is 100 and sigma is 15?
items.why: With n = 36, SE = 2.5 and z = 3.2. With n = 9, SE = 5 and z = 1.6. The same difference is more surprising with a larger sample.

items.q: With df = 9 and alpha = .05 two-tailed, the critical t is 2.262. What is the decision?
o: Retain the null, because 1.98 is below 2.262
Reject the null, because t is positive
Reject the null, because the mean difference is 5
items.why: The obtained t falls outside the critical region. The exact p value is about .08.

items.q: A factorial design has an advantage over two separate one-factor studies because it
o: Tests how factors combine, which separate studies cannot
items.why: Only a factorial design can reveal whether one factor's effect depends on another.

o: The association between variables, not causation
items.why: Experimental manipulation is needed for causal claims.

items.q: Why not run several t tests instead of one ANOVA for three groups?
o: Each extra test raises the overall Type I error rate
items.why: With three tests at .05 the chance of at least one false alarm is about 14 percent, not 5.

items.q: A student computes z = (60 minus 50)/10 = 1 and says "60 is 1 point above the mean." What is wrong?
o: The z of 1 means one standard deviation, which here is 10 points
The score is below the mean
items.why: Always translate z back to units. One SD equals 10 raw points in this example.

items.q: A histogram has a long tail to the left, and most scores are bunched at the high end. The skew is
items.why: Skew is named for the tail. A long left tail means negative skew, and the mean falls below the median.

o: The overall effect of one factor, averaging across the levels of the other
The effect of both factors together
The difference within a single cell
items.why: It is evaluated using the marginal means.

items.why: t = 3.0/1.212 = 2.474 with df = 12 minus 1 = 11. The critical t at .05 two-tailed is 2.201, so the result is significant (p = .031).

items.q: A study finds r = +.62 between hours studied and exam score. What proportion of exam score variability is accounted for by study time in this linear relationship?
items.why: .62 squared = .384. The other roughly 62 percent comes from everything else, including prior knowledge and test conditions.
